summary:
North Dakota stands under the United States national framework for passports, entry screening and federal identity documents; the findings below are specific to the state.

A national anti-trans legal-risk assessment dated July 2026, built from five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric scoring the most severe bills, lists North Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults, and among the states that prohibit any change to birth certificates. The assessment states that this prohibition forces transgender people to disclose their status when presenting documents.

Birth-certificate gender markers are effectively closed. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document tracker records that North Dakota's 2023 law bans all gender-marker changes on birth certificates with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery, a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than in many other states, and marks North Dakota a negative-law state. The regulations accompanying the 2023 statute were rejected, leaving in place a 2008 regulation restricting changes to those who have undergone a sex conversion operation.

Driver's licences and state ID cards follow a separate and lower threshold: the Department of Transportation updates the gender marker on receipt of a physician or therapist letter stating that the applicant has completed a permanent gender role transition.

North Dakota statutes do not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity. Employment discrimination is addressed federally under Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020), and city-level protections exist in Grand Forks for city employees and applicants and in rental housing from 2013. An April 2021 state law allows student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students.

Providing gender-affirming care to minors is illegal under a bill passed by a veto-proof majority on 5 April 2023.

Two bills signed into law in April 2023 ban individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletics in schools and in higher education respectively. A 2021 bill to the same effect passed the House 69 to 25 and the Senate 27 to 20 but was vetoed by Governor Doug Burgum on 21 April 2021.

An April 2023 law, effective 1 July, explicitly allows restriction of transgender individuals' public bathroom usage in many state-run facilities.

HB 1522 (2023), an act relating to preferred pronouns and accommodations to a transgender student, carried a penalty provision and an emergency clause, was signed by the governor, and had its last official action filed with the Secretary of State on 9 May 2023. The corresponding May 2023 law, effective 1 July, forbids schools and government entities from requiring or prohibiting preferred pronoun use and requires disclosure of transgender students to parents in state-run schools. A March 2023 bill requiring parental and administrative approval for preferred pronoun use in state-run schools and classrooms had been vetoed.

North Dakota's hate-crime law does not cover gender identity, while federal prosecution for crimes motivated by gender identity has been available since the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of 2009. A June 2021 committee regulation bans conversion therapy by social workers, psychologists and counsellors.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, following prior constitutional and statutory restriction to one man and one woman; proceedings in Ramsay v. Dalrymple were suspended in January 2015. The Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians legalised same-sex marriage on its reservation by 6 to 2 in August 2020.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 assessment's placement of North Dakota among the worst states is derived from a legislative rubric applied to bill tracking, not from per-capita or population-adjusted incident data, so the ranking indicates the volume and severity of enacted measures rather than a measured rate of harm.

A 2022 Public Religion Research Institute poll found 78 percent of North Dakota residents supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, with 22 percent opposed.

In July 2020 North Dakota Republican delegates voted for the party's election platform opposing any civil-rights protections for LGBTQ people and accusing transgender people of preying on women and LGBTQ people of recruiting children. Many Republican delegates condemned the platform, and Governor Doug Burgum opposed it as divisive, stating that all North Dakotans deserve to be treated equally and live free of discrimination.

A March 2023 bill that would allow businesses to refuse service on any grounds based on religious objection alone passed the legislature and awaited gubernatorial action; the sources do not record its final disposition.
localsOnly:
Residents have no state statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations; the practical floor is federal Title VII under Bostock v. Clayton County, supplemented by municipal rules for city employees and applicants and rental housing in Grand Forks from 2013.

Adoption is permitted with no express statutory ban on LGBTQ people or same-sex couples, but state law expressly allows private adoption agencies to discriminate on the basis of sincerely held religious belief. A 1980s supreme court ruling had made parental sexual orientation decisive in custody cases because of societal prejudices; that precedent was reversed in 2003.

Family-law provisions available to residents include recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent after donor insemination irrespective of marital status, express permission for gestational surrogacy for intended parents whether same-sex or different-sex, and prohibition of traditional surrogacy.

Conversion therapy is banned for social workers, psychologists and counsellors under a June 2021 committee regulation, while the state hate-crime statute still excludes gender-identity-motivated violence.

Several tribal nations within North Dakota maintain distinct traditions of gender-nonconforming roles, including third-gender people also called two-spirit, recorded as skuxát among the Arikara, miati and mihdeke among the Hidatsa and Mandan, and wįktą, winkta and wíŋkte among the Assiniboine, Dakota and Lakota. The sources state that perceptions of gender and sexuality within these communities differ from those of residents of European descent, both historically and at present.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not state whether the 2008 regulation requiring a sex conversion operation remains the operative birth-certificate rule alongside the 2023 statute, given that the accompanying regulations were rejected. Both instruments are described, and their relationship is not sourced.

Unresolved: whether HB 1522 (2023) and the May 2023 pronoun and disclosure law described in the record are the same enactment is not established by the sources; they are reported separately here.

Unresolved: no enforcement instance of HB 1522's penalty provision is documented in the inventory, and no dated incident of violence against a transgender person in North Dakota appears in the sources, so no incident-level risk statement can be made for the state.

Unresolved: the final disposition of the March 2023 religious-refusal service bill is not recorded in the sources.
